Efficiency here is the fraction of the power that ends up in the external resistors rather than in the cell, and since every term in both powers carries a factor $I^2$, the current cancels and the efficiency is just the ratio of the external resistance to the total resistance, $10.0/10.5$. That is 95.2%, and it does not depend on the e.m.f. at all.

Part (e) asks for a maximum, not a value, so it cannot be answered by substituting into the equations already set up; the candidate has to decide what is varying. With $R$ as the variable, the power is $E^2R/(R+4.5)^2$, and the maximum falls at $R = 4.5$ $\Omega$, that is at $R_1 + r$. The result generalises: the power transferred to a load is greatest when the load resistance equals the resistance of everything else in the circuit. The maximum is 2.0 W, which is less than the 1.96 W + 1.31 W the two original resistors were dissipating between them, because the load here is a single resistor carrying the whole current.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.subtopic: C.4 Standing waves on a string fixed at both ends
questions.question:
A string of length 1.20 m and mass 3.60 g is fixed at both ends and set vibrating by a small oscillator attached at one end. The figure shows the mode of vibration that is produced when the oscillator is driven at 240 Hz. The string is under tension and vibrates in the plane of the page. The mass of the string is small compared with the masses that maintain the tension, so the tension may be taken as constant. Answer all parts with reference to the figure, and give numerical answers to three significant figures.

(a)

Determine the wavelength of the waves travelling along the string in this mode of vibration.

[2]

(b)

Calculate the speed of the transverse waves travelling along the string.

[2]

(c)

Calculate the tension in the string, stating the value of the mass per unit length that you use.

[3]

(d)

Determine the frequency of the fundamental mode of this string.

[2]

(e)

The oscillator frequency is now changed to 320 Hz while the tension is kept the same. Determine the harmonic that is produced, and explain why this frequency, and no neighbouring frequency, can produce a standing wave on this string.

[4]
questions.answer:
(a) The string is fixed at both ends, so both ends must be nodes and the length of the string must contain a whole number of half-wavelengths. (M1) Counting the antinodes in the figure gives three, so the string holds three half-wavelengths and $3\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}\right) = 1.20$ m. Therefore $\lambda = \frac{2 \times 1.20}{3} = 0.800$ m. (A1) The nodes lie at the two ends and at 0.400 m and 0.800 m from one end, which is what the figure shows.

(b) The wave equation for a travelling wave is $v = f\lambda$, and the frequency of the standing wave equals the frequency of the travelling waves that compose it, so $v = 240 \times 0.800 = 192$ m s$^{-1}$. (M1)(A1) This is the speed at which a disturbance travels along the string, not the speed of any material point of the string, whose motion is transverse and much slower.

(c) The mass per unit length of the string is $\mu = \frac{m}{L} = \frac{3.60 \times 10^{-3}}{1.20} = 3.00 \times 10^{-3}$ kg m$^{-1}$. (M1) For a stretched string the wave speed is related to the tension by $v = \sqrt{T/\mu}$, so $T = \mu v^2$. (M1) Substituting, $T = (3.00 \times 10^{-3})(192)^2 = (3.00 \times 10^{-3})(3.6864 \times 10^4) = 111$ N. (A1) A tension of about a hundred newtons is plausible for a string weighing a few grams, which is a useful check on the arithmetic.

(d) The fundamental mode is the longest wavelength the string can support, with a single antinode and one half-wavelength across the fixed length. (M1) Hence $\lambda_1 = 2L = 2.40$ m and $f_1 = \frac{v}{\lambda_1} = \frac{192}{2.40} = 80.0$ Hz. (A1) Equivalently, the mode shown is the third harmonic, so $f_1 = \frac{240}{3} = 80.0$ Hz, and the two routes must agree.

(e) The standing waves possible on a string fixed at both ends have frequencies $f_n = \frac{nv}{2L}$, which are the integer multiples of the fundamental 80.0 Hz. (M1) Since $\frac{320}{80.0} = 4$ exactly, the driving frequency coincides with the fourth harmonic, so a standing wave with four half-wavelengths and four antinodes is produced. (A1) At any other frequency the waves reflected from the fixed ends return out of phase with the driver. (M1) The reflected wave then interferes destructively at the driver instead of reinforcing it, so the amplitude does not build up and only a small forced vibration remains. (A1) Resonance requires the round trip along the string to be a whole number of wavelengths, which is exactly the condition that the driving frequency be a harmonic; a frequency a few hertz away would leave the string forced but not resonant.
questions.explanation:
The figure gives the shape of a mode, not a measurement, so the first thing to do is to read it as a boundary-condition statement. Both ends are fixed, so both are nodes, and the number of half-wavelengths that fit between them is an integer. Counting the antinodes in the figure gives three, so the string holds three half-wavelengths, and since the string is 1.20 m long each half-wavelength is 0.400 m and the wavelength is 0.800 m. A candidate who reads three wavelengths instead of three half-wavelengths gets 0.400 m, which then makes the speed wrong by a factor of two.

With the wavelength and the driving frequency the wave equation gives the speed immediately, and with the speed and the linear density it gives the tension. The linear density is where the units do the damage: the string has a mass of 3.60 g, which is $3.60 \times 10^{-3}$ kg, and dividing by 1.20 m gives $3.00 \times 10^{-3}$ kg m$^{-1}$. Using grams throughout gives a tension a hundred thousand times too large, which is the sort of answer a candidate should notice is absurd for a string.

Part (d) reverses the harmonic series. The mode that is drawn is the third harmonic at 240 Hz, so the fundamental is 240/3 = 80.0 Hz, and the string can vibrate at 80, 160, 240, 320 Hz and so on.

Part (e) is the conceptual centre of the item. The temptation is to assume that a string driven at any frequency will vibrate at that frequency, which is true of the forced vibration but not of the standing wave. A standing wave requires the waves reflected from the ends to return in phase with the driver, and that happens only when the round-trip path length is a whole number of wavelengths. Here 320 Hz is exactly four times the fundamental, so it is the fourth harmonic and a standing wave with four antinodes appears. A frequency of 310 Hz would force the string to move, but the reflected waves would arrive out of phase, the amplitude would not build up, and no stable standing wave would form.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.subtopic: A.1 Kinematics: reading a velocity-time graph
questions.question:
The figure is the velocity-time graph for an object moving in a straight line. The object accelerates uniformly from rest, then travels at a constant velocity, then decelerates uniformly until it is momentarily at rest, and then continues to accelerate in the opposite direction. The letters A, B, C and D label the four regions between the line and the time axis: A, B and C lie above the axis and D lies below it. Because the motion is along a single straight line, the sign of the velocity gives the direction of travel, and the area between the line and the axis counts as positive displacement above the axis and negative displacement below it. Questions (a) to (e) all refer to this graph, each is worth one mark, and numerical answers should be given to three significant figures.

(a)

Determine the displacement of the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph, taking account of the direction of travel.

[1]

(b)

Determine the acceleration of the object at the instant t = 11 s, at which the object is momentarily at rest.

[1]

(c)

Calculate the average velocity of the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph.

[1]

(d)

Calculate the total distance travelled by the object over the whole 12 s interval shown on the graph.

[1]

(e)

Determine the speed of the object at the instant t = 9.5 s.

[1]
questions.answer:
(a) A. The displacement is the signed area between the graph and the time axis. From 0 to 3.0 s the region is a triangle, $\frac{1}{2}(3.0)(9.0) = 13.5$ m; from 3.0 s to 8.0 s it is a rectangle, $(5.0)(9.0) = 45$ m; from 8.0 s to 11 s it is a triangle, $\frac{1}{2}(3.0)(9.0) = 13.5$ m; from 11 s to 12 s it is a triangle below the axis, $\frac{1}{2}(1.0)(-3.0) = -1.5$ m. Adding, $13.5 + 45 + 13.5 - 1.5 = 70.5$ m. (A1)

(b) A. The acceleration is the gradient of the graph. From 8.0 s to 12 s the graph is one straight line, so the gradient is constant over that whole interval and is $(v_{12} - v_8)/(12 - 8) = (-3.0 - 9.0)/4.0 = -3.0$ m s$^{-2}$. The velocity happens to be zero at t = 11 s, but that says nothing about the gradient: the object is passing through rest, not sitting at it. (A1)

(c) A. Average velocity is displacement divided by time, $70.5/12 = 5.875$, i.e. 5.88 m s$^{-1}$. (A1)

(d) A. Distance travelled treats every area as positive, so $13.5 + 45 + 13.5 + 1.5 = 73.5$ m. The difference between this and the answer to (a) is twice the final area, 3.0 m, which is the ground covered while moving backwards and then given up again. (A1)

(e) A. On 8.0 s to 11 s the velocity falls at 3.0 m s$^{-2}$, so $v(9.5) = 9.0 - 3.0(9.5 - 8.0) = 9.0 - 4.5 = 4.5$ m s$^{-1}$. Since the velocity is still positive there, the speed equals the velocity. (A1)
questions.explanation:
A velocity-time graph is worth more than the formula it encodes, and this cluster is built to make that visible. The single graph carries four pieces of information that candidates routinely run together, and each question isolates one of them.

The first distinction is between signed and unsigned area. The region D lies below the time axis, so it represents motion in the negative direction, and the displacement it contributes is negative. Distance travelled, by contrast, counts every area as positive. Parts (a) and (d) ask for the two quantities and differ by exactly twice the final triangle, 3.0 m. A candidate who gets (a) and (d) both right understands the distinction; a candidate who gets (d) right and (a) wrong has found the distance when asked for the displacement.

The second distinction is between a quantity and its rate of change. At t = 11 s the object is momentarily at rest, and the tempting answer to part (b) is that the acceleration is zero because the velocity is. That is wrong, and the graph shows why: the line is straight from t = 8 s all the way to t = 12 s, so the gradient, and therefore the acceleration, is the same at t = 11 s as it is at t = 9 s. The object does not pause at rest; it passes through. This is the same error as assuming that a ball thrown vertically upwards has zero acceleration at the top of its flight.

The third distinction is between the two averages. Average velocity uses displacement, average speed uses distance, and because the object reverses, the two differ. Part (c) asks for the velocity and offers the speed as a distractor.

Part (e) checks whether the candidate can read an intermediate value off the graph rather than only its endpoints, and the distractors correspond to reading the deceleration as ending at t = 12 s instead of t = 11 s, which is the commonest way to misplace the zero crossing.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.question:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on kinematics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Use $g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ where a numerical value is needed, and give each answer to three significant figures.

(a)

A projectile is launched from level ground at $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $40^{\circ}$ above the horizontal. Air resistance is negligible. What is the speed of the projectile at the highest point of its path?

[1]

(b)

Two projectiles are launched from the same point at the same speed, one at an angle $\theta$ and the other at $90^{\circ}-\theta$, where $\theta \ne 45^{\circ}$. Both land at the launch height. Which statement is correct?

[1]

(c)

A ball is released from rest at the same instant that an identical ball at the same height is fired horizontally. Both balls experience air resistance with a drag force proportional to their speed. Which statement is correct?

[1]

(d)

A particle moves along a straight line at $8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for $3.0\ \mathrm{s}$ and then at $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in the opposite direction for $2.0\ \mathrm{s}$. What are its average speed and its average velocity over the $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$?

[1]

(e)

A boat whose speed in still water is $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ must cross a river $120\ \mathrm{m}$ wide in which the current flows at $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the shortest possible crossing time, and how far downstream does the boat land?

[1]
questions.answer:
(a) A. Resolve the launch velocity: the horizontal component is $30\cos 40^{\circ}=22.98$ and the vertical component is $30\sin 40^{\circ}=19.28$. The horizontal component is constant throughout, and at the highest point the vertical component has been reduced to zero by gravity, so the speed there is simply $22.98$, i.e. $23.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) The near miss is C, which reports the component that has vanished rather than the one that remains.

(b) A. The range is $v^{2}\sin 2\theta/g$, and $\sin\bigl(2(90^{\circ}-\theta)\bigr)=\sin(180^{\circ}-2\theta)=\sin 2\theta$, so the two ranges are equal. The flight time is $2v\sin\theta/g$, which is larger for the larger angle. (A1) Distractor D inverts both conclusions and C gets only the time right.

(c) A. With drag $\mathbf{F}=-k\mathbf{v}$ the component equations are separate: vertically, $m\dot v_{y}=-kv_{y}-mg$ for both balls, with the same initial condition $v_{y}=0$. The horizontal motion therefore cannot influence the descent, and both land together. (A1) This is a genuinely counter-intuitive result and B, C and D are all attempts to make the longer or faster trajectory cost time.

(d) A. Distance $=8.0(3.0)+4.0(2.0)=24+8=32\ \mathrm{m}$; displacement $=24-8=16\ \mathrm{m}$. Dividing by $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$ gives an average speed of $6.4$ and an average velocity of $3.2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) The pair is what is being tested: many candidates compute one correctly and then quote it twice.

(e) A. The crossing time is the width divided by the component of the boat's velocity perpendicular to the bank. That component is greatest, at the full $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, when the boat points straight across, so $t=120/4.0=30\ \mathrm{s}$ and the drift is $3.0\times30=90\ \mathrm{m}$. (A1) D is the trap: $45\ \mathrm{s}$ and landing opposite is a correct calculation of the *shortest path*, since the resultant speed is then $\sqrt{4.0^{2}-3.0^{2}}=2.65\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $120/2.65=45\ \mathrm{s}$, but the question asks for the shortest time.
questions.explanation:
This cluster is built around one idea: in kinematics, the first move is always to decide which quantities are shared and which are not. In (a) the horizontal component survives and the vertical one does not. In (b) complementary launch angles share a range because the range depends on $\sin 2\theta$, but they do not share a flight time because that depends on $\sin\theta$. In (c) a horizontally fired ball shares its entire vertical motion with a dropped one, and the surprise is that this remains true when linear drag is present, because the drag then acts independently on each component. That last point is the conceptual peak of the cluster: most students have been taught the vacuum case and assume that adding air resistance must break the tie, when in fact it depends on the drag law.

Items (d) and (e) target the same separation instinct in a computational setting. In (d) the distance and the displacement differ by $16\ \mathrm{m}$, and a candidate who computes only one of them halves the question. In (e) the shortest time and the shortest path are different journeys, and the boat cannot achieve both; the $45\ \mathrm{s}$ option is a correct calculation of the wrong thing, which is the most reliable way to separate a candidate who has understood the vector structure from one who has only memorised a formula. A guessing student has no easy route here, because the four options in (e) are all internally consistent descriptions of a real journey.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme B: The particulate nature of matter
questions.question:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on thermodynamics. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Throughout, take the gas to be ideal unless a question says otherwise, and remember that the first law relates the change in internal energy to both the thermal energy transferred and the work done. Use $R = 8.31\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$ where it is needed.

(a)

A gas is compressed adiabatically. Which statement about the gas is correct?

[1]

(b)

A gas absorbs $500\ \mathrm{J}$ of thermal energy and expands, doing $200\ \mathrm{J}$ of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?

[1]

(c)

A heat engine takes in $900\ \mathrm{J}$ from a reservoir at $600\ \mathrm{K}$ and rejects heat to a reservoir at $300\ \mathrm{K}$. It does $300\ \mathrm{J}$ of work in each cycle. What are its actual efficiency and the maximum efficiency possible between these temperatures?

[1]

(d)

One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ from a volume $V$ to a volume $2V$. How much work is done by the gas?

[1]

(e)

Which of the following processes is permitted by the second law of thermodynamics?

[1]
questions.answer:
(a) A. Adiabatic means $Q=0$, so the first law $\Delta U = Q - W_{\text{by}}$ becomes $\Delta U = -W_{\text{by}} = W_{\text{on}}$. Compressing the gas means work is done *on* it, so $\Delta U>0$ and the temperature rises. (A1) B confuses adiabatic with isothermal and D then inherits that confusion.

(b) A. With $W_{\text{by}}=+200\ \mathrm{J}$ and $Q=+500\ \mathrm{J}$, $\Delta U = 500-200=+300\ \mathrm{J}$. (A1) The sign convention is the whole question: B adds, C keeps the magnitude but flips the sign.

(c) A. The achieved efficiency is $\eta = W/Q_{\text{in}} = 300/900 = 0.333$. The Carnot limit depends only on the reservoir temperatures: $\eta_{C}=1-T_{C}/T_{H}=1-300/600=0.500$. (A1) The two numbers answer different questions and D, at $67\%$, comes from subtracting the achieved efficiency from one and so reporting the rejected fraction of the input as if it were the useful output.

(d) A. For an isothermal change $pV=nRT$ is constant, so $W=\int p\,dV = nRT\ln(V_{2}/V_{1}) = 8.31\times300\times\ln 2 = 1.73\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$. (A1) B is $nRT$ with the logarithm omitted, and C treats the pressure as falling linearly so that a mean pressure could be used.

(e) A. Free expansion into a vacuum does no work and involves no heat transfer, so $\Delta U=0$ for an ideal gas, but the entropy increases because the gas occupies a larger volume. The second law forbids the other three: B is the Clausius statement, C is the Kelvin statement, and D contradicts the entropy form directly. (A1)
questions.explanation:
This cluster exists because the first law of thermodynamics is a signed equation in three quantities and students routinely lose marks on the signs rather than on the physics. Items (a) and (b) isolate exactly that: in (a) the compression means the work term enters with the opposite sign to an expansion, and in (b) the gas both receives heat and spends energy doing work, so the change in internal energy is the difference, not the sum. The distractors are the four ways of getting a sign wrong.

Items (c) and (d) isolate a different and more interesting confusion: the difference between what a device actually achieves and what is theoretically available. In (c) the engine's real efficiency and the Carnot efficiency are computed from entirely different information, one from the energy flows and the other from the reservoir temperatures alone, and a candidate who reaches for the temperatures to compute the achieved efficiency has conflated them. In (d) the work of an isothermal expansion is logarithmic, which surprises students who expect a pressure-times-volume product; the $2.49\ \mathrm{kJ}$ distractor is $nRT$ and the $1.25\ \mathrm{kJ}$ distractor is the mean-pressure approximation that would be correct if the pressure fell linearly with volume, which it does not. Item (e) closes the cluster by asking which process the second law permits, and the correct answer is the one that increases entropy, which is the unifying idea behind the whole cluster.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.question:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on the wave model. Each one stands alone, so you can attempt any of them without the others. Unless a question says otherwise, the frequency of a wave is fixed by its source and does not change when the wave crosses a boundary between two media.

(a)

A transverse pulse travels along a stretched string whose far end is rigidly clamped. What happens to the pulse when it reaches the clamped end?

[1]

(b)

A water wave of frequency $2.0\ \mathrm{Hz}$ travels from deep water, where its speed is $0.80\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, into shallow water, where its speed is $0.60\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What happens to its wavelength?

[1]

(c)

Two coherent sources emit in phase. At a point P the difference in the distances from the two sources to P is $1.5\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength. What is observed at P?

[1]

(d)

Two coherent waves of amplitudes $3A$ and $A$ superpose in phase. What is the ratio of the intensity of the resultant wave to the intensity of the larger wave on its own?

[1]

(e)

Unpolarised light of intensity $I_{0}$ is incident on a polariser. A second polariser, whose transmission axis is at $60^{\circ}$ to the first, is placed after it. What is the intensity of the light emerging from the second polariser?

[1]
questions.answer:
(a) A. A clamped end is a fixed boundary: the displacement there must be zero at every instant, so the reflected pulse must cancel the incident one at that point, which means it is inverted. A free end gives an uninverted reflection instead. (A1) The distinction is the boundary condition, not the size of the pulse.

(b) A. Frequency is set by the source and is unchanged on crossing the boundary. With $v=f\lambda$, the deep-water wavelength is $0.80/2.0=0.40\ \mathrm{m}$ and the shallow-water wavelength is $0.60/2.0=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. (A1) C is the common error: it is the frequency that is invariant, not the wavelength.

(c) A. A path difference of $1.5\lambda$ equals three half-wavelengths, an odd number, so the phase difference is $3\pi$ radians, equivalent to $\pi$, and the superposing arrivals cancel. (A1) C is the trap worth noting: it names the correct phase difference and then draws the opposite conclusion.

(d) A. Amplitudes add before squaring: the resultant is $3A+A=4A$, so the resultant intensity is proportional to $16A^{2}$ while the larger wave alone is proportional to $9A^{2}$, giving $16/9=1.78$. (A1) B omits the squaring and C treats the waves as incoherent, which would give $(9+1)/9=1.11$ and would be right only if the phase relationship were random.

(e) A. The first polariser transmits half the unpolarised intensity, giving $I_{0}/2$ of plane-polarised light. Malus' law then multiplies by $\cos^{2}60^{\circ}=0.25$, so the final intensity is $I_{0}/2\times0.25=0.125\,I_{0}$. (A1) B, at $0.25\,I_{0}$, is Malus' law applied without the initial halving.
questions.explanation:
This cluster tests the wave model through a series of distinctions that are easy to state and easy to forget under pressure. In (a) the boundary condition decides the reflection, and a fixed end is not a free end. In (b) exactly one of frequency and wavelength is invariant across a boundary, and it is the one students are least inclined to hold constant because they can see the wavelength change. In (c) the classification depends on whether the path difference is an odd or an even number of half-wavelengths, and the $1.5\lambda$ value is chosen so that the wrong counting gives a confident wrong answer.

Items (d) and (e) are where the cluster earns its difficulty, because both hinge on an operation that must be done before the comparison. In (d) amplitudes must be added first and only then squared, because intensity is proportional to the square of the resultant amplitude; adding the intensities instead throws away the cross term, which is the entire interference effect and is larger than one of the two intensities on its own. In (e) there are two stages and the first is the one that gets forgotten: unpolarised light loses half its intensity at the first polariser, and Malus' law applies only to the polarised beam that emerges. Both items reward a candidate who writes down what is being combined before reaching for a formula, and both punish one who pattern-matches the surface features of the question.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme A: Space, time and motion
questions.question:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on special relativity. Each stands alone, so any one of them can be attempted without the others. Unless a question says otherwise, $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the Lorentz factor is $\gamma = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$. All frames referred to are inertial, and every speed quoted is measured relative to the frame named in that question rather than relative to any other object.

(a)

A spacecraft receding from Earth at $0.60c$ switches on a forward-pointing lamp. What speed does an observer on Earth measure for the light leaving the lamp?

[1]

(b)

A muon has a mean lifetime of $2.2\ \mathrm{\mu s}$ measured in its own rest frame. What mean lifetime does a laboratory observer measure for muons travelling at $0.98c$?

[1]

(c)

A rod of proper length $100\ \mathrm{m}$ moves lengthwise at $0.80c$ past a stationary observer. What length does that observer measure?

[1]

(d)

Two spacecraft approach each other head-on, each moving at $0.75c$ relative to Earth. At what speed does the pilot of one see the other approach?

[1]

(e)

An electron has total energy $1.533\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Taking its rest energy as $0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$, what is its speed?

[1]
questions.answer:
(a) A. The second postulate fixes the speed of light at $c$ for every inertial observer, so the source's motion is irrelevant and no transformation is needed. (A1) B and C are the two Galilean habits, and they are listed because $1.60c$ and $0.40c$ are the numbers a student actually produces rather than numbers chosen at random.

(b) A. The lifetime quoted for the muon at rest is the proper time, so it is the shortest of all measured lifetimes and the laboratory value is larger: $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-0.98^{2}} = 5.03$, giving $5.03 \times 2.2 = 11\ \mathrm{\mu s}$. (A1) This is the effect that lets muons created in the upper atmosphere reach sea level at all.

(c) A. The proper length is measured in the rod's own frame, and the moving observer measures $L = L_{0}/\gamma = 100/1.67 = 60\ \mathrm{m}$. (A1) The identification of which length is proper is the whole question; the division is trivial once that is settled.

(d) A. Neither spacecraft's frame is the Earth frame, so the speeds must be combined with $u' = (u+v)/(1+uv/c^{2}) = 1.50/1.5625 = 0.96c$. (A1) The denominator is what keeps the result below $c$.

(e) A. $\gamma = E/E_{0} = 1.533/0.511 = 3.00$, and inverting $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}$ gives $\beta = \sqrt{1-1/9} = 0.943$. (A1) The three distractors are all the same omission at different depths.
questions.explanation:
This cluster is built on a single observation: at $0.6c$ and above, the Galilean answer and the relativistic answer differ by far more than experimental uncertainty, so a student cannot fall back on intuition. Every item has a Galilean reading that produces a clean number, and every one of those numbers is offered as a distractor. That is deliberate. A multiple-choice item on relativity is only diagnostic if the wrong options are the ones a candidate actually derives, and $1.50c$, $100\ \mathrm{m}$ and $1.60c$ are all derived, not guessed.

The two items that carry the most weight are (c) and (d), because both require a decision about frames before any formula is applied. In (c) the candidate has to identify which of the two lengths is the proper length, and the word 'proper' is doing real work: it means measured where the object is at rest, not 'the one mentioned first'. In (d) the candidate has to notice that the Earth frame is neither of the two frames being compared, so the speeds quoted cannot simply be added. Both errors are errors of setup, and both are invisible in the final arithmetic because the arithmetic is easy.

Item (e) is included because the relationship between energy and speed is where relativity stops being a set of formulae and becomes a single quantity, $\gamma$, from which everything else follows. Once the candidate sees that the total energy divided by the rest energy *is* the Lorentz factor, the rest is algebra, and the same move works for momentum and for the Doppler factor. That unification is what the syllabus is reaching for, and it is worth saying out loud when going through the item.

questions.subject: Physics HL
questions.topic: Theme C: Wave behaviour
questions.question:
Five independent multiple-choice questions on the Doppler effect. Each stands alone. Take the speed of sound in air as $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the speed of ultrasound in soft tissue as $1540\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ where those are needed. For electromagnetic radiation use $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

(a)

A siren emitting $500\ \mathrm{Hz}$ moves at $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ towards a stationary observer. What frequency does the observer hear?

[1]

(b)

The same $500\ \mathrm{Hz}$ siren is now stationary and the observer moves towards it at $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What frequency does the observer hear?

[1]

(c)

A hydrogen line with laboratory wavelength $656\ \mathrm{nm}$ is measured in the spectrum of a galaxy at $689\ \mathrm{nm}$. What is the motion of the galaxy along the line of sight?

[1]

(d)

An ultrasound probe emits $5.0\ \mathrm{MHz}$ at $60^{\circ}$ to blood flowing at $0.40\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the magnitude of the Doppler shift in the reflected signal?

[1]

(e)

An aircraft flies at $510\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in air where the speed of sound is $340\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. What is the half-angle of the Mach cone it produces?

[1]
questions.answer:
(a) A. A moving source compresses the wavefronts ahead of it, so the wavelength in the medium is shortened while the observer samples at the usual rate: $f' = fv/(v-u_{s}) = 500 \times 340/310 = 548\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (A1) Note that the denominator contains the source speed, because it is the spacing of the crests that has changed.

(b) A. A moving observer meets unchanged wavefronts more often, so it is the numerator that changes: $f' = f(v+u_{o})/v = 500 \times 370/340 = 544\ \mathrm{Hz}$. (A1) The two answers differ by about $4\ \mathrm{Hz}$ for identical speeds, and that difference is the whole point of asking both questions: the situations are physically different even though the relative speed is the same.

(c) A. The wavelength is longer than the laboratory value, so the galaxy is receding. The redshift is $z = (689-656)/656 = 0.0503$, and since $z \ll 1$ the recession speed is $zc = 1.51 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (A1) Direction first, magnitude second: the sign of the wavelength change carries the physics and is worth stating before any arithmetic.

(d) A. Reflection imposes the shift twice and only the along-beam component contributes, so $\Delta f = 2fv\cos 60^{\circ}/c = 2 \times 5.0\times10^{6} \times 0.40 \times 0.500/1540 = 1.30\ \mathrm{kHz}$. (A1) The factor of two is not a correction: the blood is first a moving observer and then a moving source.

(e) A. The wavelets emitted along the flight path superpose on a cone whose half-angle satisfies $\sin\theta = v_{\text{sound}}/v_{\text{source}} = 340/510 = 0.667$, giving $\theta = 41.8^{\circ}$. (A1) A faster aircraft makes the cone narrower, which is the check that rules out the cosine.
questions.explanation:
The first two items are deliberately the same question twice with the motion moved from one side to the other, and the intended lesson is that the answers are not the same. When the source moves, the wavelength in the medium is changed and the observer's sampling rate is not; when the observer moves, the reverse holds. The two expressions are $fv/(v-u_{s})$ and $f(v+u_{o})/v$, they give $548\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $544\ \mathrm{Hz}$ for identical speeds, and a candidate who memorised a single 'Doppler formula' has no way to choose between them. That is why both numbers appear in both items: recognising the correct one is the test, not computing it.

Item (d) is the one where two independent factors have to be applied and neither is optional. The factor of two arises because the moving blood is first a moving observer of the incoming beam and then a moving source of the reflected one, so the shift is imposed twice. The cosine arises because only the component of velocity along the beam produces a shift at all, which is why clinical probes are held at a known angle and why $60^{\circ}$ rather than a rounder angle was chosen for the item. A candidate who gets one factor and not the other arrives at $2.6\ \mathrm{kHz}$ or $0.65\ \mathrm{kHz}$, both of which are offered, and both of which are wrong for a reason the candidate can be told.

Item (e) closes the cluster by asking for a decision about trigonometry rather than a substitution. Drawing the wavelets shows that the sine, not the cosine or tangent, relates the two speeds to the cone angle, and the physical check is the trend: a faster aircraft should give a narrower cone. A candidate who checks the trend catches the cosine error even if the diagram did not.
